title: The winter descent
line: On the longest night, go down with the torch, and sow a virtue.
intro: For Athena the winter solstice, the longest night, is a privileged gate and not a misfortune: the soul’s deepest dive, the dark night before rebirth, after which the sun climbs again. Athena’s inner work for it is a descent: like Persephone, with the hero’s torch, you face one of your monsters, trace its roots, uproot it and sow a virtue in its place.
does: On the solstice evening, by a single light, face one passion, trace its roots and sow a virtue.
trains: Facing what lives in the dark without fear, and turning it into virtue.
steps: On the evening of the solstice, keep about an hour free and find a quiet place. Switch off the phone and dim the lights: darkness, Athena says, means introversion, the time to turn inward.
Light one candle or a small lamp: the hero’s torch. Sit with it for a few minutes, and let yourself go down, as Persephone descends, into what you usually keep out of sight.
Name one of your monsters: a passion that has ruled you this year (a fear, a rage, a jealousy, an envy, a craving). Look at it face to face, without fear, wishing for its transformation.
Trace its roots: in which events, which family patterns, perhaps which ancestors did it begin? Write down what you find in your notebook.
Light it with awareness, and choose what you will sow in its place: a virtue, love, kindness, cooperation or truth. Write it beneath the roots.
Sit a little longer in the dark around the light. At rock bottom, Athena says, the choice is “light or nothing”; from this night the sun climbs again, and the inner sun is born.
If you can, tend what you sowed with one small act on each of the four days that follow, up to 25 December: for the Pythagoreans four is establishment, and what was done in the depths is made firm.
note: What did you find in the dark, and what will you sow in its place?
